items.title: HolmesGPT keynote and lightning talk: from AI diagnosis to guarded auto-remediation
items.who: Microsoft (Jorge Palma) and Robusta (Natan Yellin, Arik Alon)
items.summary: A sponsored keynote on March 24, 2026 demonstrated HolmesGPT, the open-source troubleshooting agent in the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) sandbox, correlating logs, metrics and cluster state, then moving to remediation under remediation policies, role-based access control (RBAC) limits, approval workflows and audit trails. The abstract promised to be candid about large language model (LLM) non-determinism. A March 23 lightning talk for site reliability engineers (SREs) by Robusta's chief technology officer (session attachment named 'holmesgpt auto remediation') argued for starting with pre-approved, human-in-the-loop fixes and only gradually moving toward full autonomy.
items.operationalIdea: Roll out agent remediation in stages: read-only diagnosis first, then pre-approved fixes that a human confirms, and only later autonomous actions, with every action inside an RBAC boundary and written to an audit trail. Treat the agent's root cause as a hypothesis to confirm, because the speakers themselves flag non-determinism.

items.title: How HolmesGPT builds an evidence chain: an agentic, read-only investigation loop
items.summary: HolmesGPT breaks a question into a task list, decides which data to fetch, runs targeted queries (Prometheus metrics, Kubernetes events, logs, pod specs), correlates them (for example spotting that a recent deployment changed the image), and returns a plain-language diagnosis with suggested fixes. Its base access is read-only and inherits the caller's RBAC permissions; it ships many built-in data-source integrations (Prometheus, Loki, Tempo, Datadog, Helm, ArgoCD and more) and works with existing runbooks and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, and can use any LLM provider, including models run inside the cluster. Each tool subprocess is memory-capped so a huge query cannot crash the agent.
items.operationalIdea: Give the agent the same read-only service account an on-call engineer would use for triage, and feed it your existing runbooks so its investigation follows the team's known steps. When a tool result comes back truncated or out of memory, narrow the query (namespace, label, shorter time window) rather than raising limits.
items.appFeatureHint: Render the investigation as an ordered evidence chain: each step shows the query run, the data source, and what it found, ending in the correlated change (for example 'image changed in deploy X at 14:02'). Let users click any step to see the raw evidence.

items.title: How agentic diagnosis fails: HolmesGPT's own benchmark, run five times per scenario
items.summary: The project's benchmark published March 14, 2026 ran 20 Kubernetes and cloud troubleshooting scenarios five times each (100 graded runs per model), graded by a judge model. Overall pass rates ranged from 70% to 89% across five frontier models, and the same scenario often passed only some of the five runs. Historical log questions were weakest: Loki log scenarios passed 10% to 40% of runs.
items.operationalIdea: Do not trust a single agent run as the root cause. Run it more than once or ask for evidence links, and be most skeptical when the answer depends on historical logs, which the project's own tests show is the weakest area.
items.appFeatureHint: Add a 'consistency' indicator: re-run the diagnosis two or three times and show whether the probable root causes agree, and flag log-history-based conclusions as lower confidence.

items.summary: On March 10, 2026, two weeks before KubeCon, Microsoft made Azure SRE Agent generally available. It runs multi-layer investigations across apps, platform and infrastructure, keeps a knowledge base built from past incidents, and lets teams choose autonomy from recommend-only up to automated responses within guardrails. items.title: How agentic diagnosis fails: HolmesGPT's own benchmark, run five times per scenario
items.who: HolmesGPT project (benchmark results in its docs)
items.summary: The project's benchmark, generated March 14, 2026, ran 20 Kubernetes and cloud troubleshooting scenarios five times each, giving 100 graded runs per model. A judge model (gpt-4.1) graded the runs. Overall pass rates ranged from 70% to 89% across five frontier models, and many scenarios passed only some of the five runs. items.title: OpenTelemetry cardinality capping: 'Metrics That Lie' (default 2,000 series per metric, overflow silently merged)
items.who: Cijo Thomas (Microsoft), OpenTelemetry; KubeCon EU 2026 lightning talk
items.summary: Microsoft's KubeCon EU 2026 session list included a lightning talk by Cijo Thomas, 'Metrics That Lie', on OTel's cardinality capping, which he later wrote up on the OTel blog (August 6, 2026). The OTel metrics specification sets a default of 2,000 attribute combinations per metric stream; extra combinations are folded into one overflow data point tagged otel.metric.overflow=true with their attributes removed, so totals stay right but filtered or grouped views can undercount. items.title: OpenTelemetry Collector memory_limiter refuses data above its soft limit, and data is lost if the sender doesn't retry
items.summary: The memory_limiter processor starts refusing data once memory use passes the soft limit. It returns a non-permanent error and expects the upstream component to retry. Above the hard limit it also forces garbage collection. If the component in front of it does not retry, the data is permanently lost, and the README warns that long refusal periods can end in dropped data. The batch processor (default send_batch_size 8192, timeout 200ms) belongs after memory_limiter and any sampling.

A gateway Collector then passes its soft limit and starts refusing OpenTelemetry Protocol (OTLP) data. Any sender that doesn't retry loses exactly the incident's spans and logs. Size Collectors for incident-level volume, set GOMEMLIMIT as the README recommends, and alert on refusals.

items.title: Tail sampling needs every span of a trace on one Collector, which means a load-balancing exporter layer
items.summary: Head sampling decides early, without seeing the whole trace, so it cannot guarantee that every trace containing an error is kept. The tail_sampling processor can, but every span of a trace must reach the same Collector instance. That requires a first layer using the load-balancing exporter, which routes traces by trace ID by default. Defaults are decision_wait 30s and num_traces 50000. When more traces are in memory than num_traces, some are dropped before they can be sampled. By default the load-balancing exporter does not re-route data to a healthy endpoint when delivery fails.
items.operationalIdea: Scaling a tail-sampling Collector from 1 to 3 replicas behind an ordinary Kubernetes Service splits each trace across pods, so 'keep all error traces' rules see partial traces and decide wrongly. Put a load-balancing exporter layer in front, routed on traceID through a headless service or the k8s resolver. During traffic spikes, watch sampling_trace_dropped_too_early and turn on exporter queue and retry.

The batch processor (default send_batch_size 8192, timeout 200ms) belongs after memory_limiter and any sampling.

A gateway Collector then passes its soft limit and starts refusing OpenTelemetry Protocol (OTLP) data. Any sender that doesn't retry loses exactly the incident's spans and logs. Size Collectors for incident-level volume, set GOMEMLIMIT as the README recommends, and alert on refusals.

items.title: Tail sampling needs every span of a trace on one Collector, which means a load-balancing exporter layer
items.summary: Head sampling decides early, without seeing the whole trace, so it cannot guarantee that every trace containing an error is kept. The tail_sampling processor can, but every span of a trace must reach the same Collector instance. That requires a first layer using the load-balancing exporter, which routes traces by trace ID by default. Defaults are decision_wait 30s and num_traces 50000. When more traces are in memory than num_traces, some are dropped before they can be sampled. By default the load-balancing exporter does not re-route data to a healthy endpoint when delivery fails.
items.operationalIdea: Scaling a tail-sampling Collector from 1 to 3 replicas behind an ordinary Kubernetes Service splits each trace across pods, so 'keep all error traces' rules see partial traces and decide wrongly. Put a load-balancing exporter layer in front, routed on traceID through a headless service or the k8s resolver. During traffic spikes, watch sampling_trace_dropped_too_early and turn on exporter queue and retry.
items.appFeatureHint: In the stack recommendations, add a 'tail sampling readiness' check: more than one Collector replica with no traceID-routed load-balancing layer means error traces will be missing.

items.title: Azure Monitor managed service for Prometheus: 1M active series and 1M events per minute per workspace, and data collection rule caps that cannot be raised
items.summary: Each Azure Monitor workspace allows 1,000,000 active time series (series reported in the last ~12 hours) and 1,000,000 events ingested per minute. Both can be raised on request. Each data collection rule (DCR) is capped at 15,000 ingestion requests per minute and 50 GB per minute, and those caps cannot be raised. Queries can span at most 32 days, and data is kept for 18 months. Ingestion is throttled when limits are reached, and the workspace publishes utilization metrics. Pricing is based on ingestion and query, with no storage charge.
items.operationalIdea: Because 'active' covers the last ~12 hours, a rollout that changes pod names, or a crash loop creating new pods, keeps old series counted for half a day. A few churny deploys in a row can push a workspace into throttling. Alert on Active Time Series % Utilization and request an increase before a migration. Since the DCR caps can't be raised, plan to spread very large clusters across more DCRs or workspaces (an inference from the fixed caps).
items.appFeatureHint: For Azure stacks, project active series over a 12-hour window from the deploy history in the Helm diff and show headroom against 1M per workspace.

items.title: Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus: 50M active series per workspace, but sudden jumps get throttled long before that
items.summary: Each workspace defaults to 50,000,000 active series (a series is active if it had a sample in the past 2 hours), adjustable up to 1.5 billion. Capacity scales automatically between 2M and 50M based on the last 30 minutes of usage. Throttling can still happen if usage doubles, or rises by 10M or more, above that 30-minute baseline; there is no throttling below 2 million series. The ingestion rate defaults to 1,666,666 samples per second, set automatically to 1/30 of the active-series limit up to that figure. Throttled data appears as DiscardedSamples (reason rate_limited) in CloudWatch. Billing counts each metric sample ingested. The pricing page's worked example uses $0.90 per 10 million samples for the first 2 billion; the page labels it an example and does not state the region.
items.operationalIdea: The ceiling is rarely the problem. The burst rule is. Moving a whole fleet onto one workspace, or a deploy that doubles series within 30 minutes (for example, adding a container label to every histogram), can be throttled while still far below quota, once the workspace is above 2 million series. Ramp up gradually and set a CloudWatch alarm on DiscardedSamples with reason rate_limited.

items.title: Google Cloud Managed Service for Prometheus: billed per sample ingested, with histograms charged per non-empty bucket
items.summary: Managed Service for Prometheus is billed by samples ingested, not bytes. The rate is $0.06 per million samples for the first 50 billion, $0.048 per million for the next 50 to 250 billion, $0.036 per million for 250 to 500 billion, and $0.024 per million beyond 500 billion. items.summary: Publishing OpenTelemetry metrics to CloudWatch costs $0.50 per GB ingested. That includes 15 months of storage and carries no charge for API calls, storage or number of unique series. Ingested volume is measured on the uncompressed OTLP payload, attributes included. A typical data point with 10 to 15 attributes is 300 to 600 bytes. Classic CloudWatch metrics are billed per metric: the page's worked example uses $0.30 per metric for the first 10,000.
items.operationalIdea: With per-GB pricing, a new attribute never hits a series quota and never adds a billed metric. Instead, every attribute you attach makes each data point larger, so the bill grows with the size of the label set. Trim Kubernetes resource attributes in the Collector before export. On classic CloudWatch metrics, each new metric adds a per-metric charge instead.

items.title: Microsoft at KubeCon Europe 2026: GPU metrics in managed Prometheus, metric collection set by custom resources, Hubble cardinality controls, HolmesGPT in CNCF
items.who: Microsoft (Brendan Burns, Kubernetes co-founder and Microsoft Corporate Vice President)
items.summary: Brendan Burns's KubeCon Europe 2026 post (March 24, 2026) announces several things. Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) now sends GPU utilization into managed Prometheus and Grafana. Operators can choose which container-level metrics are collected using Kubernetes custom resources. Microsoft contributed controls to Cilium for limiting Hubble (Cilium's network observability layer) metric cardinality. Azure Kubernetes Fleet Manager adds cross-cluster networking through a managed Cilium cluster mesh. The post also states that HolmesGPT has joined the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) as a Sandbox project; Microsoft's March 10 preview already called it a CNCF sandbox project, so that join predates the event.
items.operationalIdea: On Azure, the answer to hitting workspace series limits is moving from 'request an increase' toward 'collect less at the source': custom resources that switch off container-level metrics, and Hubble cardinality controls for network metrics. Platform teams can add these to the cluster config before onboarding GPU or network telemetry, which are high-volume sources.
